questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the amendment that set the voting age at eighteen
questions.stem: Memo section 1.1 asks which amendment lowered the voting age to eighteen nationwide.

options.text: The Twenty-sixth Amendment, ratified in 1971, set the voting age at eighteen.
The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, set the voting age at eighteen.
options.misconception: confuses the voting rights amendment with the age amendment

options.text: The Nineteenth Amendment, ratified in 1920, set the voting age at eighteen.
options.misconception: attributes the age limit to the women's suffrage amendment

options.text: The Twenty-fourth Amendment, ratified in 1964, set the voting age at eighteen.
options.misconception: confuses the poll tax amendment with the age amendment

questions.explanation: The Twenty-sixth Amendment of 1971 bars denying the vote on age grounds to citizens eighteen and older. It grew out of the argument that those old enough to serve in the military should be able to vote, and it applies in every state.
questions.hint: One amendment deals with age, one with money.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the poll tax ban to small registration charges
questions.stem: Memo table 1.2 lists registration fees of zero, zero, two, and three dollars across four states. What constraint applies?

options.text: Only fees above five dollars can be a poll tax, so these amounts are all lawful.
options.misconception: invents a dollar threshold for the poll tax ban

options.text: A payment may not be a condition of voting in a federal election, whatever the amount.
Only states that charge registration fees are subject to the Twenty-fourth Amendment.
options.misconception: assumes states without fees are exempt from scrutiny

options.text: Fees are lawful because they are collected before election day, not at the polls.
options.misconception: believes the timing of the charge removes it from the ban

questions.explanation: The poll tax ban looks at whether money is a condition of voting in a federal election, so small charges are not automatically safe. A fee collected well before election day can still be a payment attached to voting.
questions.hint: Focus on the condition, not the size.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what federal examiners did in covered counties
questions.stem: Memo task 1.3 asks the team to explain what federal examiners did in covered counties.

answer.exemplar: Federal examiners were sent by the United States to monitor elections in covered jurisdictions, and they could register eligible citizens, oversee voting, and certify the count. Their presence replaced state registrars who had used literacy tests and intimidation, and that shift in who controlled the process removed a large share of the disenfranchisement federal law was written to end.

questions.explanation: Examiner power put federal officials in charge of registration and voting in covered counties. Saying examiners only observed misses their power to register voters and to certify results, which was what broke the barrier practice.
questions.hint: They did more than watch.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute how early a voter registered relative to a deadline
questions.stem: Memo line 1.4 states that state law allows voter registration up to 30 days before an election. A citizen registers 45 days before election day. By how many days did the citizen register before the deadline?
questions.explanation: Forty five days before the election minus the 30 day deadline equals 15 days of margin. Reading the rule as a minimum rather than a latest date is the usual source of error, since it flips the direction of the subtraction.
questions.hint: Subtract the deadline from the registration date.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a reduction in federally staffed polling places

stimulus.body: The appendix notes that federal observers were sent to 120 polling places in the last federal cycle and to 90 polling places in the most recent one, after a court decision narrowed the list of covered jurisdictions. The memo proposes planning new early voting sites anyway.

questions.stem: Memo appendix on observers notes coverage falling from 120 polling places to 90. What is the most defensible reading?

options.text: Federal observers were eliminated, so the state no longer must follow federal standards.
options.misconception: treats reduced staffing as repeal of federal standards

options.text: The drop proves that the covered jurisdictions were removed for political reasons.
options.misconception: asserts partisan motives without any evidence

options.text: The 30 site difference reflects a fall in the number of voters casting ballots.
options.misconception: reads a staffing figure as a voter count

options.text: Fewer federally staffed sites remain, so local planning must supply reliable access on its own.

questions.explanation: The memo documents a reduction in federally staffed polling places after a court narrowed the list of covered places. That changes the level of federal staffing support, not the underlying requirement that elections be administered lawfully.
questions.hint: Staffing levels and legal duties are different things.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an inconsistent set of overseas ballot counts
questions.stem: Memo table 1.6 lists 1,800 overseas ballot requests, 1,900 returned ballots, and 1,950 registered overseas voters. What is the defensible reading?

options.text: Overseas turnout was 91 percent, because 1,800 of 1,950 registered voters requested.
options.misconception: treats a ballot request as a vote cast

options.text: Returned ballots exceed requests, so the counts contain an error or overlap.
About 50 overseas voters received two ballots each by mistake.
options.misconception: assumes double voting to explain the gap

options.text: The ballot count shows a sharp rise against the previous cycle.
options.misconception: claims a trend the single table cannot show

questions.explanation: Requests and returns cannot exceed one another in a clean count, so the table contains an error or double counting. A ballot request is not a vote, which defeats the turnout reading, and one table cannot show a trend.
questions.hint: Check the two counts against each other.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why equal population is the measure of fair districts
questions.stem: Memo task 1.7 asks the team to explain why equal population is the measure of fair districts.

answer.exemplar: Representation is granted to people, not to territory, so a district with twice as many residents should not carry the same voting weight as one with half as many. Requiring near equal populations makes each legislator answerable to roughly the same number of constituents, and it stops a map from quietly diluting a group's influence by packing its voters into oversized districts.

questions.explanation: The principle is one person, one vote applied to geography. Treating land area as the measure would let sparsely populated regions dominate, and the rule also limits the manipulative use of district size.
questions.hint: People, not square miles.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute how far a district falls below a population target
questions.stem: Memo line 1.8 notes that a county of 54,000 voters is split into three districts of 18,000 each. The state charter targets 20,000 voters per district. By how many voters does each district fall short of the target?
questions.explanation: Twenty thousand minus eighteen thousand is a shortfall of 2,000 voters in each district. The usual mistake is dividing the county population by four instead of comparing each district with the target.
questions.hint: Compare each district with the charter target.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Test a district against a minority population threshold

stimulus.body: The appendix describes a county where one district contains 62 percent minority voters and two districts nearby hold 14 and 11 percent. A second appendix reports that the same county's overall minority share is 31 percent, and the county's charter requires districts to deviate from the average population by no more than five percent.

questions.stem: Planner appendix describes a district at 62 percent minority and a county at 31 percent. What is the sound inference?

options.text: The 62 percent district proves the county's overall share is higher than 31 percent.
options.misconception: infers the county average from one district

options.text: The district is required to match the county's 31 percent share by law.
options.misconception: invents a proportional requirement for each district

options.text: The 62 percent district is packed, since it holds far more of the group than the county average.
The district's population must be at least 40 percent above the average.
options.misconception: claims the population deviation is forced by the group share

questions.explanation: A district that holds twice the county's share of a group is the signature of packing. Nothing in the appendix requires districts to match the county average, and the population limit operates on residents rather than on group shares.
questions.hint: Compare the district with the county's own share.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the electoral vote total needed to win the presidency
questions.stem: Memo section 1.10 asks which total wins the presidency under the Electoral College system.

options.text: A majority of the popular votes cast nationwide across all states.
options.misconception: assumes a national popular vote decides the presidency

options.text: A plurality of electoral votes, so 100 votes would be enough.
options.misconception: confuses a plurality with the required majority

options.text: A majority of the states, so 26 states would elect the president.
options.misconception: reduces the election to a count of states

options.text: A majority of electoral votes, which is 270 of the current 538.

questions.explanation: A candidate must win a majority of electoral votes, currently 270 of 538, not the most votes cast. There is no national popular vote requirement, and a plurality of electoral votes is not enough.
questions.hint: Majority of votes, not of votes cast.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the restriction on age-based denial of the vote
questions.stem: Memo task 2.1 asks the team to explain why the voting age was lowered to eighteen.

answer.exemplar: The Twenty-sixth Amendment was ratified in 1971 after members of Congress argued that young citizens who were drafted to fight in Vietnam should be allowed to vote at home. Setting the age at eighteen also pushed states toward a uniform rule, since before it each state chose its own voting age and those choices often restricted younger citizens.

questions.explanation: The amendment answered the mismatch between being drafted and being allowed to vote, and it set a uniform national floor at eighteen. It reaches state elections, not just federal ones.
questions.hint: It followed a mismatch between service and suffrage.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the revenue raised by a poll tax
questions.stem: Memo line 1.12 notes that Congress forbade poll taxes for federal elections. If a state kept a $3.25 poll tax and 12,000 voters paid it, how much money would the state have collected?
questions.explanation: Twelve thousand voters times 3.25 dollars equals 39,000 dollars. The trap is dividing instead of multiplying, or reading the amount as 3.2, which produces a slightly wrong total.
questions.hint: Multiply the rate by the number of payers.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the practices the Voting Rights Act targeted

stimulus.body: An archival note on the county's election history records that before federal examiners arrived, three registrars in the county refused to register Black applicants who could not pass a reading test on a state-provided passage. Two of those registrars were later prosecuted, and one county commissioner resigned over the practice.

questions.stem: Archival note describes registrars using a reading test to block registration. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The barrier was administrative in practice, carried out by local registrars under state law.
The barrier was a federal rule that only applied outside the South.
options.misconception: makes the test a federal rather than a state practice

options.text: The barrier had already been declared unconstitutional by the Court in 1965.
options.misconception: pins the timing of a ruling the note does not mention

options.text: The barrier disappeared once the county adopted the machine ballot.
options.misconception: attributes the change to voting equipment

questions.explanation: The note shows state law and local registrars producing the barrier in practice, which is why federal examiners and prosecutions were needed. Nothing in the note connects the practice to equipment changes or to a specific court ruling date.
questions.hint: Look at who actually administered the rule.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the federal ceiling on state registration deadlines
questions.stem: Memo section 1.14 asks which statement about registration deadlines is accurate.

options.text: Federal law sets a single nationwide registration deadline for every election.
options.misconception: assumes one national deadline exists

options.text: A state sets its own deadline, and federal law caps how close to an election it may fall.
States may set any deadline, even one on election day itself.
options.misconception: assumes no ceiling on registration deadlines

options.text: Registration deadlines apply only to presidential elections, not state races.
options.misconception: limits deadlines to federal elections

questions.explanation: Federal law places a ceiling on how close to an election a registration deadline can fall, usually thirty days, and states set their own deadlines within that limit. The ceiling protects time for voter rolls to be prepared, and it applies to state elections too.
questions.hint: States choose, but a limit caps the choice.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret changes in covered jurisdictions and observer sites
questions.stem: Memo table 1.5 counts federal observer sites at 120 last cycle and 90 this cycle, and lists covered jurisdictions at 4 then 2. What does the table show?

options.text: The number of jurisdictions fell but federal staffing stayed flat, so coverage widened.
options.misconception: contradicts the figures the table gives

options.text: Fewer observer sites means observers stopped monitoring any polling place.
options.misconception: reads a decline as an end to the program

options.text: The drop in sites proves that voter turnout fell by the same share.
options.misconception: equates staffing figures with turnout

options.text: Both federal staffing and the number of covered jurisdictions fell after the 2013 ruling.

questions.explanation: The table shows both counts falling together, which is what the coverage and preclearance changes would predict. Staffing levels say nothing about how many people voted, and neither count fell to zero.
questions.hint: Read both columns, not just one.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute how late an overseas ballot missed a receipt deadline
questions.stem: Memo line 1.16 states that an overseas voter's ballot must be received 45 days before the election. A citizen living abroad mailed the ballot 50 days before the election. By how many days did the citizen miss the deadline?
questions.explanation: Fifty days before the election minus the 45 day receipt deadline equals 5 days late. Mailing 50 days out sounds early in absolute terms, which is why people misread the rule as a mailing deadline rather than a receipt deadline.
questions.hint: The rule is about receipt, not mailing.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess a modest population deviation and its justification

stimulus.body: A survey note reports that the state's two districts hold 51,200 and 48,800 residents, a gap of 2,400 people around 4.8 percent of the 50,000 average. The note adds that one district crosses a county line because the other district's lines would split a town of 3,100 residents.

questions.stem: Survey note reports a 2,400 person gap between two districts. What is the sound reading?

options.text: The gap is large enough to void the map, because districts must be identical.
options.misconception: insists on exact population equality

options.text: The gap is modest, and the town split offers a legitimate reason for the deviation.
The gap is fine because county lines always control district boundaries.
options.misconception: makes county lines the controlling rule

options.text: The gap shows the map was drawn to favor a political party.
options.misconception: infers partisan intent from a population figure

questions.explanation: Substantial equality allows modest deviations backed by legitimate reasons such as keeping a community whole. Exact mathematical equality is not required, and a population gap alone proves nothing about partisan intent.
questions.hint: Substantial equality, not identical numbers.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish packing from cracking in district maps
questions.stem: Memo section 1.18 asks how packing differs from cracking when a map is drawn.

options.text: Packing concentrates a group's votes in one district, while cracking spreads them thin across several.
Packing spreads a group's votes across districts, while cracking concentrates them in one.
options.misconception: reverses the two techniques

options.text: Packing means drawing long districts, while cracking means drawing compact ones.
options.misconception: confuses the tactics with district shape

options.text: Packing and cracking are the same technique applied to different groups of voters.
options.misconception: treats both tactics as identical in effect

questions.explanation: Both tactics seek the same partisan outcome by manipulating the geographic distribution of a group's votes. Packing concentrates the group so it wins one seat, and cracking dilutes it so it wins none in the surrounding districts.
questions.hint: One concentrates, one dilutes.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a district against a minority population threshold
questions.stem: Memo table 1.9 lists a district of 8,400 voters of whom 3,150 are minority voters against a 35 percent threshold. What does the table show?

options.text: The district fails the threshold, because 3,150 voters is fewer than a third of 8,400.
options.misconception: misreads the threshold as one third

options.text: The district passes only if turnout among minority voters rises by two points.
options.misconception: confuses a population threshold with a turnout measure

options.text: The district meets the threshold, because 3,150 of 8,400 voters is 37.5 percent.
The district is within five voters of the threshold and so falls short.
options.misconception: treats the share as a rounding argument

questions.explanation: 3,150 divided by 8,400 equals 0.375, or 37.5 percent, which clears the 35 percent requirement. These thresholds are measured in population, so turnout figures do not affect the calculation.
questions.hint: Divide the group count by the total.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a winner-take-all state can swing a presidential result
questions.stem: Memo task 2.0 asks the team to explain why a state with winner take all electoral voting can swing a presidential result.

answer.exemplar: In a winner take all state, every electoral vote goes to the statewide winner, so a narrow statewide margin can deliver a large block of electoral votes at once. That is why a candidate can lose the national popular vote and still win the presidency, and it is why campaigns spend heavily on close states rather than only on the biggest ones.

questions.explanation: The allocation rule, not the headcount of votes, decides how many electors a candidate gets. Explaining a loss in the popular vote requires the state level allocation rule, not a claim about the national tally.
questions.hint: The unit of allocation is the state.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Summarize the scope and effect of the voting age amendment

stimulus.body: An agenda note for a public meeting lists an item supporting the voting age amendment. It states that citizens who could be drafted to serve at eighteen should be able to vote at eighteen, and it notes that the measure lowers the age without touching state rules on registration or identification.

questions.stem: Agenda note argues for lowering the voting age. Which statement about the amendment is accurate?

options.text: It set the minimum voting age at eighteen and applies to state elections as well as federal ones.
It set the minimum voting age at eighteen only for presidential and congressional races.
options.misconception: limits the amendment to federal elections

options.text: It lowered the age to eighteen only where a state already had that age.
options.misconception: describes the amendment as optional for states

options.text: It raised the minimum age to twenty-one for state and local elections.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the change

questions.explanation: The amendment bars denial of the vote on age grounds to citizens eighteen and older in any election, primary included. It sets a floor rather than leaving each state's age intact, and it leaves registration and identification rules where they were.
questions.hint: A floor, and it reaches state races too.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a charge that falls outside the poll tax ban
questions.stem: Memo section 2.2 asks which of these the poll tax ban does not cover.

options.text: A fee of two dollars per ballot demanded before a federal ballot is counted.
options.misconception: reads the amendment as covering any fee before voting

options.text: A state fee that a person pays to obtain a birth certificate used for voter registration.
A dollar charge levied on each voter who casts a ballot in a federal election.
options.misconception: treats a per ballot charge as a poll tax

options.text: A payment of five dollars collected from every voter before the polls open.
options.misconception: treats a poll day payment as outside the ban

questions.explanation: The Twenty-fourth Amendment bars a payment as a condition of voting in a federal election. A fee for obtaining a birth certificate is a cost of documentation rather than a condition of casting a ballot, so the amendment does not reach it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the payment is attached to voting itself.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret examiner counts and state coverage figures
questions.stem: Memo table 2.3 lists literacy test usage in 12 states before 1965 and federal examiner assignments in 46 counties after it. What does the table show?

options.text: The examiners outnumbered the states, so every county became covered.
options.misconception: confuses counties with states in the coverage count

options.text: The examiners replaced state registrars in all fifty states.
options.misconception: overstates examiner coverage nationwide

options.text: Federal enforcement followed a state practice that the table shows was widespread in 1964.
Twelve states and forty six counties show the same ratio, so the figures are consistent.
options.misconception: claims a false numerical consistency

questions.explanation: The two counts describe different units of government, and the drop in literacy testing after federal enforcement shows the practices targeted. Examiner assignments in covered counties did not extend to every state.
questions.hint: The two figures count different things.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the administrative reason for a deadline ceiling
questions.stem: Memo task 2.4 asks the team to explain why a registration deadline cannot fall right before the election.

answer.exemplar: A deadline set only days before election day would leave election officials almost no time to compile the list of eligible voters, verify addresses, and resolve challenges to that list. The federal ceiling on deadlines protects that administrative window, so a state may choose an earlier cutoff but may not compress the process to the final days.

questions.explanation: The ceiling is about the time officials need to run an accurate election, not about discouraging registration. A state may set a more generous deadline, and the rule does not cap how early a deadline may be.
questions.hint: Think about the voter's roll, not the voter.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the percentage drop in federally staffed polling places

questions.explanation: Thirty fewer polling places out of 120 is 30 divided by 120, which is 25 percent. A common error is dividing 30 by 90, the new count, which gives 33.3 percent and overstates the reduction.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the rule for counting a mailed overseas ballot
questions.stem: Memo section 2.6 asks how a state treats a ballot mailed by a service member on overseas duty.

options.text: The ballot is counted only if a local official witnesses the overseas voter sign it.
options.misconception: invents a witnessing requirement for overseas ballots

options.text: The ballot is counted if it reaches the local office by the state's deadline, which must be reasonable.
The ballot is counted only if the service member votes in person at a military base.
options.misconception: assumes service members must vote on base

options.text: The ballot is counted only if it arrives before the general election rather than after.
options.misconception: ignores the extension of the deadline for mailed ballots

questions.explanation: Federal law requires states to let absent service members and overseas voters request and return a ballot, and to provide a reasonable deadline for it to arrive. Counting the ballot depends on the state's deadline rather than on a witness or a personal appearance.
questions.hint: Arrival time is what matters.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute a population gap as a share of the average district
questions.stem: Memo table 2.7 shows district populations of 51,200 and 48,800 people. How should the planner read that gap?

options.text: The gap of 2,400 people is a clear violation because districts must be identical.
options.misconception: insists on exact equality of population

options.text: The gap of 2,400 people is under 5 percent of the average district population, a modest deviation.
The gap of 2,400 people shows the map was drawn for partisan advantage.
options.misconception: reads any deviation as partisan intent

options.text: The gap of 2,400 people proves the districts were drawn along racial lines.
options.misconception: infers racial intent from population figures alone

questions.explanation: Substantial equality allows small deviations, and a gap of 2,400 against an average near 50,000 is well within what courts treat as modest. Population figures alone do not establish partisan or racial intent.
questions.hint: Compare the gap with the average of 50,000.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a map dilutes a group's voting strength
questions.stem: Memo task 2.8 asks the team to explain how a map can dilute a group's voting strength.

answer.exemplar: A map dilutes a group by dividing the group's concentrated population across several districts, so the group forms a minority in each one and no candidate from that group can win. Cracking is the mirror image of packing, where the same population is squeezed into a single safe district, and both techniques reduce the group's chances of electing the candidate it prefers.

questions.explanation: Cracking works by spreading a group's votes thinly, while packing wins one district with overwhelming margins. Describing only the geography without the effect misses why both techniques reduce representation.
questions.hint: Follow the votes, not the lines.

questions.learningObjective: Compute how many voters a district must add to meet a threshold
questions.stem: Memo line 2.9 notes a district of 10,000 voters with 2,400 minority voters, and a charter requiring at least 2,900 minority voters. How many more minority voters must the district add to qualify?
questions.explanation: The gap between the 2,400 voters present and the 2,900 required is 500 voters. The trap is comparing 2,400 with the 30 percent threshold of 3,000 instead of the charter's stated number of voters.
questions.hint: Required minus present.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the body that chooses a president in a contingent election

stimulus.body: A county note records that the state awards its electoral votes as a unit to the statewide winner, and that in the last election the top ticket won the county by 900 votes while losing the state by 40,000 votes. The note plans a celebration for the winner's visit to the county.

questions.stem: County note describes a statewide winner who carried the county narrowly. What does the note support?

options.text: One county's margin can matter little while another state's margin can carry ten electoral votes.
The county's narrow win means the state result was calculated incorrectly.
options.misconception: treats an unsurprising allocation as an error

options.text: A county cannot influence the statewide result because votes are counted only statewide.
options.misconception: denies that local margins feed the statewide count

options.text: The county wins its ten electoral votes on its own, apart from the statewide result.
options.misconception: believes counties allocate electoral votes separately

questions.explanation: Votes are counted for the statewide race, and the county's result simply feeds into that total, but the unit of allocation is the state. That is why a narrow margin in one large state can matter more than a margin in one county.
questions.hint: The state is the unit of allocation.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read turnout data without mistaking it for eligibility
questions.stem: Memo table 3.1 gives turnout rates by age: 24 percent at eighteen to twenty-nine, and 51 percent at thirty to forty-four. What can the planner conclude?

options.text: The lower turnout shows eighteen year olds are still excluded from the vote.
options.misconception: reads low turnout as continued exclusion

options.text: Younger citizens are eligible but vote at a much lower rate, so outreach should target them.
The 27 point gap proves the voting age amendment failed and should be repealed.
options.misconception: reads turnout data as a verdict on the amendment

options.text: Turnout data shows that registration deadlines do not affect younger voters.
options.misconception: attributes a turnout gap to a specific law without evidence

questions.explanation: Turnout measures participation among eligible voters, so a low rate reflects behaviour rather than eligibility. The amendment's effect is on who may vote, and the data support targeting outreach rather than changing the law.
questions.hint: Participation is not the same as eligibility.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the poll tax ban is written as a rule about conditions
questions.stem: Memo task 3.2 asks the team to explain why the poll tax amendment targets money rather than a list of named state practices.

answer.exemplar: By banning money as a condition of voting in federal elections, the amendment reaches any payment that works the same way, whether it is called a poll tax, a registration fee, or a charge levied by a local official. Naming one device in the text would leave obvious equivalents intact, so the rule is written in terms of the condition itself.

questions.explanation: A functional ban closes the loophole that naming a specific tax would leave open. That is why the drafters spoke of money as a condition of voting rather than listing the forms a payment might take.
questions.hint: The wording covers the function, not the label.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of states that used literacy tests
questions.stem: Memo line 3.3 notes that 12 of the 50 states used literacy tests in the year before the Voting Rights Act. What percentage of the states used literacy tests?
questions.explanation: Twelve divided by 50 is 0.24, or 24 percent of the states. The usual error is dividing by the 38 states without tests, which produces a percentage of a different group than the question asks about.
questions.hint: States with tests over all states.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Determine the legal effect of a late registration

stimulus.body: The registrar's note says the county's registration deadline is 30 days before an election and that a group of nursing students at the state college registered 12 days before the election, after the deadline. The note asks whether the students can vote in the upcoming election or must wait for the next one.

questions.stem: Registrar's note describes registrations filed 12 days before the election. What is the correct answer?

options.text: The students may vote, because the state can extend a deadline when it has good cause.
options.misconception: invents a good cause extension to deadlines

options.text: The students are late for this election but their registrations stand for the next one.
The students are late and must re-register before every future election as well.
options.misconception: makes the lateness permanent and repeated

options.text: The students may vote because the deadline applies only to presidential elections.
options.misconception: limits the deadline to federal elections

questions.explanation: A registration filed inside the 30 day window is late, so it does not qualify the student for that election, but the registration is not voided. The deadline is set by state law and applies to state races as well as federal ones.
questions.hint: Late for one cycle, still on the roll.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify which jurisdictions still face federal preclearance
questions.stem: Memo section 3.5 asks which states must still seek federal preclearance for voting rule changes.

options.text: No state, because the 2013 decision ended preclearance requirements everywhere.
options.misconception: overstates the decision as ending preclearance

options.text: Only states that sued and lost in court, since others were never covered.
options.misconception: makes preclearance depend on litigation history

options.text: The states that remain covered by the coverage formula Congress set after the decision.
Only the five states that had the earliest voting rights statutes.
options.misconception: invents a criterion based on statute age

questions.explanation: After the 2013 decision the coverage formula was rewritten by Congress and the jurisdictions it covers still face preclearance. The obligation depends on coverage, not on whether a state happened to be sued.
questions.hint: Coverage decides it, not litigation history.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the safeguards that make absentee voting credible
questions.stem: Memo task 3.6 asks the team to explain why absentee and overseas voting carry extra safeguards.

answer.exemplar: A voter who votes away from the polling place cannot be watched by poll workers, so the process leans on documentation, signature requirements, and deadlines to confirm that the ballot belongs to the voter who signed it. The safeguards slow the process, but without them a mail ballot system would be open to both fraud and wrongful rejection of legitimate voters.

questions.explanation: Absentee voting trades in-person observation for documentary control, so the safeguards are what keep it credible. Saying the system needs no verification because the law trusts the voter misses the reason the rules exist.
questions.hint: Observation is traded for documentation.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the population difference between two districts
questions.stem: Memo line 3.7 gives the populations of two districts as 51,200 and 48,800 people. What is the difference in population between the two districts?
questions.explanation: Fifty one thousand two hundred minus forty eight thousand eight hundred equals 2,400 people. The trap is averaging the two figures instead of subtracting them, which gives 50,000 and answers a different question.
questions.hint: Larger minus smaller.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare a packed district with an alternative redrawing

stimulus.body: The planner's memo notes that in the pre redistricting map, one district held 78 percent minority voters while the four districts surrounding it each held between 8 and 14 percent. A second plan would keep the same population but place part of it in two adjacent districts with larger minority shares.

questions.stem: Planner's memo compares a packed district with a redrawn alternative. What does the comparison show?

options.text: The packed district maximizes minority representation because it holds the largest share of the group.
options.misconception: reads a packed seat as the strongest outcome

options.text: The packed district concentrates the group in one seat while the redraw spreads it across two.
The redraw reduces minority representation because it breaks the group into smaller pieces.
options.misconception: ignores that a split can create two winnable seats

options.text: The two plans are identical in effect because both reflect the same population totals.
options.misconception: treats equal totals as identical partisan effects

questions.explanation: Concentration and dispersion have opposite effects on how many seats a group can win, even with the same population. That is exactly why maps are examined for packing and cracking rather than only for population totals.
questions.hint: Same voters, different seats.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the purpose of a minority opportunity district
questions.stem: Memo section 3.9 asks what a minority opportunity district is intended to produce.

options.text: A district where no single racial group holds a majority of the population.
options.misconception: describes an integration requirement instead

options.text: A district where a minority group can elect its candidate of choice.
A district drawn so that each race holds an equal share of the electorate.
options.misconception: reads the label as a proportional requirement

options.text: A district in which turnout among minority voters reaches a set quota.
options.misconception: turns the label into a turnout program

questions.explanation: A minority opportunity district is drawn so that a minority group forms an effective voting majority, which lets that group elect the representative it prefers. It is not a quota on turnout and does not require any racial group to be a minority in the district.
questions.hint: Electable is the operative word.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute an electoral vote total across several states
questions.stem: Memo table 4.0 shows three states with 10, 20, and 30 electoral votes and a candidate leading each state. What does the table show?

options.text: The candidate's 60 electoral votes are enough, because 60 is a majority of the states shown.
options.misconception: counts states rather than electoral votes

options.text: The candidate's 60 electoral votes win the election outright in these three states.
options.misconception: treats a state level lead as the whole election

options.text: The candidate needs 30 more electoral votes, since each state awards one vote.
options.misconception: assumes one electoral vote per state

options.text: The candidate's 60 electoral votes fall short of the 270 needed for a majority.

questions.explanation: Electoral votes are the unit of the count, so 10 plus 20 plus 30 gives 60 votes, far short of the 270 needed. A lead in some states does not settle the election, and states carry their full electoral vote count.
questions.hint: Add the votes, then compare with 270.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the size of the voting age reduction
questions.stem: Memo line 4.1 notes that the voting age amendment lowered the minimum voting age from twenty-one to eighteen. By how many years did the amendment lower the voting age?
questions.explanation: Twenty one minus eighteen equals a three year reduction in the voting age. The trap is subtracting from the wrong baseline, such as reading the change as five years from a mistaken age of twenty three.
questions.hint: Old age minus new age.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a ballot application fee under federal voting rules

stimulus.body: The city attorney's note advises that the county still charges a two dollar fee for the ballot application form and that the money is earmarked for the county records fund. The note adds that the fee is waived for voters who file the form before the registrar's office opens on election day.

questions.stem: City attorney's note describes a two dollar ballot application fee. How should the planner treat it?

options.text: The fee looks like a poll tax in federal elections and should be reviewed for compliance.
The fee is fine because it funds county records rather than the election itself.
options.misconception: thinks the use of the money changes legality

options.text: The fee is fine because it is waived for voters who file early enough.
options.misconception: believes a waiver removes the problem

options.text: The fee is fine because the amendment bans only fees above one dollar.
options.misconception: invents a dollar threshold for the ban

questions.explanation: The poll tax ban turns on whether money is a condition of voting in a federal election, not on how small the amount is or where the money goes. A modest application fee should be reviewed rather than assumed safe.
questions.hint: Small and earmarked do not decide it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the central command of the Voting Rights Act of 1965
questions.stem: Memo section 4.3 asks what the federal voting rules required of covered jurisdictions in 1965.

options.text: That all fifty states adopt a single uniform voter registration system.
options.misconception: invents a required uniform registration system

options.text: That no state law denying the vote on race or color could take effect.
That federal examiners be appointed in every county of every state.
options.misconception: overstates the reach of examiner appointments

options.text: That state legislatures repeal their own election statutes by a two thirds vote.
options.misconception: invents a repeal procedure

questions.explanation: The Act's central command forbade state practices that denied the vote because of race or color, and it gave federal officials the tools to enforce that command in covered places. It did not demand one registration system or repeal state statutes through a supermajority.
questions.hint: The ban is on racial barriers in state law.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a table of state registration deadlines
questions.stem: Memo table 4.4 lists registration deadlines of 45, 40, 35, and 30 days before the election in four states. What does the table show?

options.text: The federal government sets every deadline, so the differences reflect record keeping errors.
options.misconception: reverses who sets the deadline

options.text: Each state sets its own deadline, and all four meet the thirty day federal ceiling.
Only one state complies, because the ceiling requires exactly thirty days in every state.
options.misconception: believes the ceiling mandates a single date

options.text: The table shows that states with larger deadlines are more accurate than others.
options.misconception: invents an accuracy ranking from deadline length

questions.explanation: States set their own deadlines within the federal limit, so differences are expected and all four listed deadlines clear the ceiling. The rule caps lateness rather than fixing one national date, and deadline length says nothing about accuracy.
questions.hint: A cap, not a single date.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe what the 2013 decision changed about preclearance
questions.stem: Memo task 4.5 asks the team to explain what changed for state changes to voting rules.

answer.exemplar: Before the 2013 decision, covered jurisdictions had to seek federal preclearance before changing their voting rules, which meant a federal court or agency reviewed the plan for discrimination. After the decision, the coverage formula was invalidated for the states it had selected, so a covered jurisdiction today changes its rules through state procedures while remaining bound by the constitutional voting rights guarantees.

questions.explanation: The decision changed the preclearance regime for covered jurisdictions but did not touch the constitutional guarantees. Saying voting rules are now entirely unregulated misses those remaining limits.
questions.hint: The oversight regime changed, the guarantees did not.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Summarize the channels federal law provides for absent voting

stimulus.body: A program note describes the county's overseas and military voting service, which accepts applications by mail and online, mails ballots to voters who qualify, and counts any ballot that arrives by the state's deadline. The note states that a voter who requested a ballot but never received one may cast a provisional ballot at the polls.

questions.stem: Program note describes the county's overseas voting service. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The service delivers ballots only to citizens who live outside the country permanently.
options.misconception: restricts the program to permanent residents abroad

options.text: The service allows only one overseas voter per household to request a ballot.
options.misconception: invents a per household limit

options.text: The service counts only ballots that arrive on election day itself.
options.misconception: narrows the count to same day delivery

options.text: The service supports request by mail, mail delivery, and a fallback ballot at the polls.

questions.explanation: Federal law supports several channels at once: requesting a ballot from abroad, receiving it by mail, and casting a ballot in person when a mailed ballot never arrives. The protections cover temporary absence and service members, not only permanent residents.
questions.hint: Several routes, one goal: a valid vote.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify a remedy that advances equal population in districts
questions.stem: Memo section 4.7 asks which change is consistent with the equal population requirement.

options.text: Adding a new district when one area's population has grown sharply.
options.misconception: reaches for a new seat instead of redrawing

options.text: Adjusting one district boundary so its population comes closer to the others.
Leaving the map unchanged because the difference is a normal result of geography.
options.misconception: accepts imbalance without analysis

options.text: Redrawing so the two dominant parties each hold half the districts.
options.misconception: treats partisan symmetry as the goal

questions.explanation: When a district's population drifts far from the others, the usual fix is to move a boundary, not to add a seat or to leave the imbalance. Partisan symmetry is a separate and much weaker argument than equal population.
questions.hint: Redraw to bring populations back together.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a table of district group shares against a county average
questions.stem: Memo table 4.8 shows four districts with minority shares of 12, 14, 15, and 68 percent in a county where the group's overall share is 29 percent. What does the table show?

options.text: The group's overall share of 29 percent means it wins three of the four districts.
options.misconception: converts a county wide share into seat totals

options.text: All four districts are legally identical because the county average is 29 percent.
options.misconception: treats a county average as a binding limit

options.text: One district is packed and the others dilute the group, which is the classic pattern.
The table shows every district is at least 12 percent minority, so the map is compliant.
options.misconception: invents a compliance standard from a raw share

questions.explanation: One district holding far more than the county share is packing, and the remaining districts dilute the rest of the group. A county wide average is not a rule that each district must match it.
questions.hint: Compare each district with the county average.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of drawing a minority opportunity district
questions.stem: Memo task 4.9 asks the team to explain the purpose of drawing a minority opportunity district.

answer.exemplar: A minority opportunity district is drawn so that a minority group, wherever it is concentrated, forms a majority or a strong plurality of the electorate, which lets that group elect the candidate of its choice rather than being packed away into a district where it is a permanent minority. The goal is an effective voice in the legislature, not a guarantee of any particular party's seat.

questions.explanation: The purpose is to make representation effective for a group that would otherwise be unable to elect its own representative. Saying the purpose is to guarantee a party seat misstates it, since the design goal concerns the group's electoral weight.
questions.hint: Effective voice, not a reserved seat.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the delegations needed to elect a president by the House
questions.stem: Memo line 5.0 notes that the House elects a president when no candidate wins a majority of electoral votes, with each state delegation voting as a unit. With 50 states, how many delegations must vote for a candidate to win?
questions.explanation: A majority of 50 states is 26 delegations, since half of 50 is 25 and a tie does not carry. The trap is answering 270, which is the electoral vote majority rather than the count of states.
questions.hint: Count states, not electoral votes.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the voting age amendment interacts with other voter rules
questions.stem: Memo section 5.1 asks how the voting age amendment interacts with state voter identification laws.

options.text: The amendment bans denial on age grounds, but it leaves other lawful qualification rules in place.
The amendment voids every state voter identification requirement.
options.misconception: treats the amendment as invalidating ID laws

options.text: The amendment requires states to let every registered voter vote without any check.
options.misconception: reads the amendment as a ban on all checks

options.text: The amendment requires states to lower any identification fee to zero.
options.misconception: invents a fee requirement from the amendment

questions.explanation: The amendment targets age-based denial of the vote and says nothing about identification, residency, or citizenship rules. Those rules can stand if applied fairly and consistently under federal and state law.
questions.hint: It speaks about age and nothing else.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a table comparing fee practices across states
questions.stem: Memo table 5.2 compares four states, showing that two charge a fee at registration and two do not. What does the table support?

options.text: Fee practices are uniform, since the table shows the same pattern in all four states.
options.misconception: reads variation as uniformity

options.text: Only states with fees have poll taxes, and the other two are certainly compliant.
options.misconception: assumes no fee proves full compliance

options.text: The fee states are more protective of voters because fees discourage fraud.
options.misconception: treats a fee as a safeguard despite the ban

options.text: Fee practices vary by state, so each must be checked against the federal poll tax rule.

questions.explanation: The table shows variation, and variation is what calls for a rule based check rather than a general assumption. A state without a visible fee could still impose a payment elsewhere, and federal law turns on the condition of voting.
questions.hint: Variation means each one needs its own check.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Voting Rights Act targeted state practices
questions.stem: Memo task 5.3 asks the team to explain why the Voting Rights Act targeted state practices rather than only voter attitudes.

answer.exemplar: The Act reached the practices that produced unequal voting, such as literacy tests, poll taxes, and intimidation at registration and at the polls, because those practices were built into state law and administration. Attacking attitudes alone would leave the barriers standing, so the drafters gave federal officials examiners, enforcement authority, and the power to review changes to voting rules in covered jurisdictions.

questions.explanation: The statute was aimed at how states administered voting, because the discrimination was institutionalized there. Saying the Act only addressed personal prejudice misses the legal practices it made enforceable.
questions.hint: The barriers lived in state administration.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute how many days late a registration was filed
questions.stem: Memo line 5.4 states that registration closes 30 days before a November 5 election. A citizen registers on October 20. By how many days did the citizen miss the deadline?
questions.explanation: Thirty days before November 5 is October 6, and October 20 falls 14 days after that. The trap is counting from October 5 or measuring the gap to the election day, which gives a different and wrong number.
questions.hint: Find the deadline date, then count forward.

questions.learningObjective: Identify voting practices that federal law still reaches

stimulus.body: A litigation summary explains that the 2013 decision held the coverage formula unconstitutional because it relied on outdated voting data from 1964. questions.stem: Litigation summary describes the 2013 holding on the coverage formula. What is the accurate consequence?

options.text: All preclearance ended in 2013, and no jurisdiction now needs federal approval for rule changes.
options.misconception: overstates the decision as ending preclearance

options.text: The 2013 decision applied to every voting practice in every state.
options.misconception: extends the ruling to all voting rules

options.text: The decision restored the 1964 coverage formula as the operative test.
options.misconception: reverses the ruling to restore the older formula

options.text: Coverage continues under the newer formula, so preclearance still applies in covered jurisdictions.

questions.explanation: The decision struck the 1964 based formula, but Congress adopted a replacement in 2006 and the covered jurisdictions kept their preclearance obligation. So the practical change was narrower than a repeal of federal oversight.
questions.hint: Read the last sentence of the summary.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute return rates for overseas ballots across counties
questions.stem: Memo table 5.6 shows requests of 400, 500, and 600 overseas ballots across three counties, with 300, 380, and 420 ballots returned. What does the table show?

options.text: Return rates of about 75, 76, and 70 percent, so the counties are broadly similar.
Return rates of about 25, 24, and 30 percent, so most overseas voters did not return.
options.misconception: reads the returned counts as a return rate

options.text: Only the third county shows a return rate worth reviewing.
options.misconception: singled out a county without a stated standard

options.text: The counties show rising return rates as the number of requests grows.
options.misconception: infers a relationship three rows cannot support

questions.explanation: Return rate is returned divided by requested, so 300 of 400 is 75 percent, 380 of 500 is 76 percent, and 420 of 600 is 70 percent. The counties are close together, and three data points cannot show a trend.
questions.hint: Divide returned by requested for each row.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how uneven population growth requires redrawing
questions.stem: Memo task 5.7 asks the team to explain what happens when a city's population grows unevenly.

answer.exemplar: When growth is uneven, districts drawn on old population figures become unequal, so the planner must redraw boundaries to bring the populations back into line. Adding a seat or leaving the imbalance alone does not fix the problem, because the requirement is about equal representation, and a district twice the size of its neighbours gives twice the weight to one community.

questions.explanation: Decennial figures force the map to be revisited whenever the population shifts. The remedy is redrawing, and describing growth alone as the reason for unequal districts misses what the map must produce.
questions.hint: Old numbers, new people.

questions.stem: Memo line 5.8 notes a plan that packs 45,000 residents into one district in a city of 120,000. An equally sized district would hold 40,000 residents. How many residents does the packed district hold beyond an equal share?
questions.explanation: Forty five thousand minus forty thousand is 5,000 residents beyond an equal share. The trap is dividing 45,000 by three or four districts instead of comparing the packed district with the equal share.
questions.hint: Packed total minus equal share.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Choose a planning response to a dispersed minority population

stimulus.body: A charter note records that the county's minority population is 34 percent of 120,000 residents and is concentrated in two municipalities. The note observes that current districts place parts of both municipalities in four separate districts, and the county's counsel notes the requirement that districts deviate from the average population by no more than five percent.

questions.stem: Charter note describes a concentrated group split across districts. What is the sound planning response?

options.text: Split the two municipalities into more districts so the group is represented everywhere.
options.misconception: recommends further dilution of a concentrated group

options.text: Add seats until each municipality has its own district, ignoring the population cap.
options.misconception: ignores the population deviation limit

options.text: Consider a district that keeps the concentrated municipalities together where population limits allow.
Do nothing, because the group's countywide share is already above a third.
options.misconception: treats a countywide share as the operative test

questions.explanation: A group concentrated in two municipalities is a candidate for a district that keeps it together, subject to the population limits. A countywide share of 34 percent is not what the requirement tests, since it measures the group's vote within a district.
questions.hint: Concentration invites a concentrated district.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the body that resolves a deadlocked presidential election
questions.stem: Memo section 6.0 asks what happens when no candidate wins a majority of electoral votes.

options.text: The House chooses the president, voting by state delegation.
The Senate chooses the president, voting by state delegation.
options.misconception: puts the contingent election in the Senate

options.text: A new election is held with new candidates until a majority appears.
options.misconception: invents a repeat election for a hung result

options.text: The Supreme Court appoints the president from among the leading candidates.
options.misconception: gives the judiciary the contingent election role

questions.explanation: A contingent election sends the choice to the House, where each state delegation votes as a unit and a majority of states is needed. The Senate runs the contingent election for the vice president, and the courts have no role in choosing a president.
questions.hint: One chamber, one vote per state.
